Chicago Reader

Chicago’s alternative newsroom

My journey into art began as a little boy with my mother. She was, in many ways, not a good mother. We kids had to fend for ourselves, enduring physical, mental, and sexual abuse from the people in her life. I have a lot of physical and mental scars from that time. Yet, some of my best memories are also from those years—of those far too few moments when my mother was sober and making art.

I would sit and watch her for hours as she worked, her fingers flying over the paper or canvas. I would ask her a litany of questions: how she did this, or why she did that. I’m middle-aged now, older than my mom was when she died, and an artist in my own right. Still, sometimes if I run into something tricky in my artmaking, I think about how she would have handled it.

I didn’t pick up a paintbrush until I was older and far away from my mother. In 1985, my mom and her boyfriend kicked me out of the house. I was a 13-year-old kid, trying to survive on my own, and I forgot all about art. In my early twenties, I found myself on death row in downstate Menard Correctional Center. We were only out of our cells for one hour a day, if we were lucky, and I found myself searching for a way to occupy my mind. My thoughts turned to my mother drawing and painting, and I decided to turn to art, drawing every day. I was terrible—I found out very quickly that I didn’t inherit any of my mother’s talents. Without any training or schooling, I had to learn everything by trial and error, spending hours every day practicing shading and perspective. It wasn’t natural for me, but I worked hard at it, and slowly, very slowly, I began to get better and branched out into inks and more. I wanted to be good—I wanted to be great.

Art has remained my refuge all these years. It’s vital to my mental health and my sanity in a place like this, and that’s true for many other people I’ve known in prison. But it can be really difficult to access the supplies needed to make it, and sharing it with people outside can sometimes be impossible.

When I started, Menard had an art room with supplies for sale. Every spare penny I had went to good paper, colored pencils, and pastels. I loved color and what I could do with it. I’d often create cards for the people in my life to make them smile and show my love.

When I got off of death row in 2001, I was sent up to Stateville Correctional Center. In Stateville, Dr. Margaret T.G. Burroughs, cofounder of the DuSable Black History Museum, had an art class every week. As you might expect, there was a waiting list. When I finally got in, Dr. Burroughs introduced me to African artists. I was amazed by the quiet power of some of the art, especially the masks she showed us. I made my own mask out of papier-mache, which in prison is wet newspaper held together with toothpaste that dries as hard as plaster. I shaped it roughly and painted it with instant coffee, so it was a deep, rich brown. Using the dye on the shells of M&M’s, I created vibrant colors. When I took the mask to Dr. Burroughs, she loved it and asked if she could keep it; I felt so much pride and humility in that moment. She made me laugh when she asked me why it smelled like coffee. When I told her that’s what I used to paint, she said it showed her I was a real artist, that I could create amazing things. It was the first time I was ever praised for my art, and coming from her, it meant the world to me.

After that, Dr. Burroughs brought me all kinds of art supplies, including oil and acrylic paints. She said she wanted to make sure I never had to use coffee and candy to paint again. At that time, I had barely used paint in my art and had never used it at all. Dr. Burroughs told me it was the best medium. She gave me a book with all the old masters: Raphael, Bottiçelli, Renoir, and Van Gogh, among others. I was captivated. She told me there’s always room for new masters. So, I set out to teach myself how to paint in oils. It was a long and frustrating process. I was used to dry mediums like drawing, and oil paint was so different: how you use it, how you make colors, how you blend, everything was new. I remember getting so frustrated one time that I ripped up the canvas and, with a few choice words, threw it on the gallery floor. But I stayed with it and learned that even if you mess up, all you have to do is let it dry and paint right over it.

I fell in love with painting landscapes, the colors I could put in the sky, the way I could make lightning look, or the crash of waves on the rocks. I painted every day, Dr. Burroughs encouraging me every step of the way. She really liked my sunsets and took several of them home with her. I was heartbroken when she passed away. I wrote a poem for her and painted a sunset over a savannah as tribute to her—a mentor to many, and the one person who encouraged and believed in me.

I eventually learned how to paint portraits, developing my own style of realism. I make art for hours every day, listening to music and just immerse myself in the process. Art is a positive, educational, inspiring thing, and for me—it’s my little bit of freedom and opportunity. It helps me cope, relieve stress, and stay positive in a place where positivity is hard to come by. It’s a shame that IDOC does not support it to the level we need. One of the hardest parts about being in prison is that anything you want to do that’s positive is met with resistance. So many steps in a positive direction is blocked.

Unfortunately, IDOC does not have any programs to promote art. Guys in prison need to find positive things to do with their time. We used to be able to purchase art supplies from Dick Blick, but IDOC has stopped that a few years ago as well. When I run out of oil paints, that’s it; there is no way for me to get more. The prison does sell some art supplies, but they’re often out of stock or not what I need.

When you leave prison, society demands that you follow the rules, grow, and become a better person than the one who went in. They expect you to turn your life around, but make it next to impossible to do so. It’s difficult to get an education or a vocation; you don’t get real mental health treatment or social training to make re-entry easier. You can’t even have the things you need to create art.

Anthony Ehlers is an activist, journalist, and artist. He graduated from Northwestern University in 2023 and is currently a teaching fellow.

Inside Voices is a series of first-person essays and reported pieces by writers impacted by the Illinois carceral system.
